groups.text: A J V M with the A O T cache still maps classes, links, interprets, and waits for the jit.
In Quarkus's benchmark, its first request took one thousand eight hundred fifty-nine ms.
A native image answered in five hundred eighty-one ms, because it did that work in the build.
The native-image builder starts at main.
It follows every method call and field access it can see, and works out which classes can show up at each call.
Code it never reaches is left out, and so are the J D K classes nothing uses.
It runs static initializers where it can, and saves their objects in the image heap.
Then it compiles every reachable method to machine code.
The binary needs no class loading, no bytecode verification, no interpreter and no jit.
This is the closed-world assumption: everything the program will run is known at build time.
The price is what the analysis can't see: reflection, proxies, resources loaded by name, JNI and serialization.
Constants are fine.
Class.forName with a literal name just works, because the build can read it.
But this decoder takes the class name from a Kafka message header.
The build can't know it.
On the J V M, Class.forName finds PaymentAuthorized on the class path and loads it.
The native binary can't load classes.
Nobody told the build about PaymentAuthorized, so the call throws MissingReflectionRegistrationError.
It's an Error: don't catch it.
You tell the build in reachability-metadata.json, on the class path.
An entry names the type and the members your code uses.
A constructor is called init.
Parameter types are fully qualified, and every method lists them, even when there are none.
The condition turns the entry on only once EventDecoder is reached.
Now PaymentAuthorized decodes as it did on the J V M.
RefundIssued isn't listed, so it still fails.
In a Quarkus app you rarely write this file.
Extensions know what their libraries reflect on, and Quarkus generates the jay-son.
For classes only your code knows about, you add RegisterForReflection.
